hyperedges.label: Primitive → utility → bridge → token → theme
hyperedges.rationale: A primitive renders Tailwind utilities; shadcn-bridge.css gives each utility a var(--token) via @theme inline; tokens.css re-points that token under [data-theme="dark"] and prefers-color-scheme; so the primitive is correct in both themes with no .dark class, no next-themes and no dark: utility, and it borrows src/ui/Button.tsx rather than shipping a second button. No pairwise edge carries the whole chain.

hyperedges.label: A clip's path: listen route → adapter → confidence gate → cost ledger
hyperedges.rationale: The transport posts multipart audio to listen; the selected adapter returns {text, confidence, seconds, provider, model}; the derived confidence meets Build Spec §5.3's 0.6 gate (null meaning unknown, which the gate must not read as low); the seconds are priced and written to the call ledger's stt_paise and stt_seconds. Transcribing is deliberately a separate failure from answering, so the whole chain runs before /turn is ever called.

hyperedges.label: Why Kannada went 86% → 100%
hyperedges.source_location: ### What was wrong, and what fixed it
hyperedges.rationale: search_menu matches a Latin-script menu and menu_vocabulary is M4, so a Kannada query returns nothing; the assistant compensated by translating and re-searching, which costs one of the four tool rounds a turn allows; because nothing in the prompt named the menu's script it only did that about half the time, so the same case passed one run and failed the next — the variance, not recognition, was the 86%. npm run trace made the round-by-round sequence visible, and two prompt lines (menu is Latin script; batch a multi-dish order) removed the variance to give 100% with zero genuine failures.

hyperedges.label: the mock-mode listen path: the transport supplies the words, everything else runs for real
dark mode arrives three ways (toggle cookie, OS media query, Tailwind dark: variant) and is kept consistent by a test rather than by the language
the ASR confidence chain: each provider's number, or its null, travels unchanged to Build Spec §5.3's 0.6 gate, and null must read as unknown rather than low

nodes.label: Repository Conventions
nodes.rationale: Conventions are stated as absolutes (TypeScript strict, UTC storage, UK English, audit log on every customer-data write) so that no reviewer has to adjudicate a judgement call at the keyboard; the file also asserts precedence — product decisions live in the Ideation file, and unstated behaviour is a stop-and-ask, not an invention.

nodes.label: Portfolio-First, Pilot-Ready Build Mode
nodes.rationale: Every external vendor sits behind an adapter with a working mock so the whole product runs end to end with no vendor account; when a real account arrives it is a new implementation plus an environment variable, never a change to calling code. This keeps the build demonstrable before any commercial relationship exists.

nodes.label: src/core Domain Logic Layer
nodes.rationale: No imports from next, react or the database — pure functions over plain data — because this is the layer the voice service's tool calls reuse at M2, so anything web-shaped in it would have to be duplicated or unpicked.

nodes.label: src/voice Call Assistant Brain
nodes.rationale: Prompt, LLM loop, tool handlers, guardrails and ledger live together and are called by API routes and by tests, never importing next, so the brain is testable without a web request.

nodes.label: contracts/ Language-Neutral Directory
nodes.rationale: Plain JSON and Markdown only, no TypeScript, because the Python voice service reads these same files at M2. Anything only TypeScript can read does not belong here.

nodes.label: contracts/voice-tools.json
nodes.rationale: Tool schemas are held in the contract file and never inlined, so the TypeScript API and the Python voice service cannot drift apart on what a tool accepts.

nodes.label: Stateless OTP Challenge
nodes.rationale: The OTP lives in a signed challenge rather than a table because Build Spec §10 gives it a ten-minute life and nothing else — a table would be state to migrate, expire and clean up for no gain.

nodes.label: Four-Table Phone Number Storage Restriction
nodes.rationale: Phone numbers exist only on customer, staff_user, platform_user and outlet; everywhere else uses phone_hash, so an erasure request has four known places to look rather than a search.

nodes.label: Definition of Done
nodes.rationale: A milestone is done when the Build Spec §14 acceptance criteria pass, not when the code exists; where a criterion says 'on a real phone', it means on a real phone.

nodes.label: ADR 0004
nodes.rationale: Cited as the decision defining M2 as the voice assistant's brain plus two vendor-free transports — a departure from the Build Spec's telephony-first M2.

nodes.label: ServeLine — Ideation.md
nodes.rationale: Canonical product thinking. Where the three documents disagree, this one wins — it is version 3 (9 September 2026) and supersedes the 28 May 2026 PRD and its research file.

nodes.label: ServeLine — Build Spec.md
nodes.rationale: Engineering brief covering how to build what Ideation decided, and nothing it did not decide; written so a two-person team or Claude Code can go from an empty repository to a ten-restaurant Bangalore pilot.

nodes.label: Document Precedence
nodes.rationale: An explicit ranking (Ideation > Build Spec > case study, with ADRs recording deliberate departures) exists so a contradiction between documents is resolved by rule rather than by whoever read last.

nodes.label: docs/adr/
nodes.rationale: Every place the repository deliberately departs from the Build Spec, and why — so the Spec can stay unedited while reality moves.

nodes.label: docs/superpowers/specs/
nodes.rationale: One design spec per milestone, agreed before implementation.

nodes.label: Actual Repository Layout
nodes.rationale: A single Next.js app with src/core, src/db, src/adapters, src/auth, src/ui and contracts/, rather than the Build Spec's apps/packages/services monorepo — the departure is recorded in docs/adr/.

nodes.label: Bangalore Seed Restaurant
nodes.rationale: The seed loads a fictional Bangalore restaurant with a three-language menu, a Direct Order Card batch and a discount code, so the whole flywheel is demonstrable from a fresh clone.

nodes.label: ServeLine
nodes.rationale: An AI-first ordering platform giving every Indian SMB restaurant its own AI ordering channel and a customer database it owns. The frame is hyper-localisation of AI: an aggregator runs one AI across thousands of restaurants in its own interest; ServeLine inverts that so each restaurant gets an AI tuned to its menu, customers, languages and neighbourhood. The hook is cost, the long-term position is ownership.

nodes.label: Order Two Belongs to the Restaurant
nodes.rationale: ServeLine deliberately claims neither demand generation nor delivery logistics; both stay with the aggregators. The narrower claim — whoever acquired the customer, the second order belongs to the restaurant — is easier to defend and is what the whole product is scoped around.
nodes.norm_label: order two belongs to the restaurant

nodes.label: Three Pillars: AI Channel, Operations, Customer Intelligence
nodes.rationale: Inseparable at MVP: an AI ordering channel without a customer database is a voice bot, and voice bots are now a rentable commodity; a customer database without an ordering channel is a CRM nobody fills in. Splitting them to reduce MVP scope would remove the only thing that compounds.
nodes.norm_label: three pillars: ai channel, operations, customer intelligence

nodes.label: Direct Order Share (North Star Metric)
nodes.rationale: The median percentage of a restaurant's total monthly orders placed through ServeLine channels. Median, not mean, so one outlier cannot carry the number; per-restaurant, so it cannot be inflated by sales headcount the way total volume can. It is also the number the restaurant itself cares about — the share of orders no longer paying commission. It replaced Monthly Direct Order Volume (rose with headcount) and then Aggregator Dependency Ratio (name inverted against its own target: going down was the good outcome).

nodes.label: North Star Denominator Problem
nodes.rationale: ServeLine sees its own orders and nothing else; the aggregator order count lives in the Swiggy and Zomato partner apps. A North Star that cannot be measured is a slogan, so manual weekly entry is P0 rather than a Phase 2 integration nicety.

nodes.label: Weekly Aggregator Order Count Entry
nodes.rationale: The owner or agent types two numbers a week from the partner apps and the dashboard nags until they do; Phase 2 pulls them through a POS or middleware integration. Risk is registered: 'North Star denominator not entered', mitigated by dashboard nag plus agent follow-up in week 2.

nodes.label: Direct Order Card
nodes.rationale: A card in the aggregator's packaging offering 10% off the next direct order. It replaced the first design, in which restaurant staff keyed aggregator customers into the database — that fails twice over, because aggregators mask customer phone numbers and no kitchen re-keys orders at 8pm on a Saturday. The card moves the work to the one person who has the number and a reason to type it, the customer, and pays them 10% to do it. The 10% is funded by the 25-28% commission the customer's later orders no longer pay, so it clears on order two.

nodes.label: Win-Back Flywheel
nodes.rationale: The flywheel needs an entry point and the entry point is the aggregator: aggregator delivers, card converts, profile is created with consent, order two comes direct, the profile deepens and the next call takes thirty seconds instead of three minutes. Every channel enriches the same phone-linked profile, so richer profiles make the AI faster and cheaper at the same time.

nodes.label: AI Call Assistant
nodes.rationale: P0 and the wedge: every restaurant is already being called and someone is already answering badly. It is also the channel no aggregator can follow the restaurant into. Hindi, English and Kannada from day one because Bangalore is the launch city.

nodes.label: Restaurant-Owned Ordering Page
nodes.rationale: One surface with two entry points, table and delivery. This replaced QR dine-in as a separate P0 feature, which was contradictory: dine-in was P0 while explicitly scoped out of the problem statement. A single page with two contexts resolves that.

nodes.label: Phone-Linked Customer Profile
nodes.rationale: Foundation for everything downstream: order history, saved addresses, dietary preferences and allergies power personalisation, the repeat-order shortcut and voice address capture. Profiles are per restaurant and nothing crosses restaurants without new consent, which matches the ownership positioning.

nodes.label: DPDP-Compliant Consent Flow
nodes.rationale: Explicit opt-in with a versioned notice on first interaction, in the customer's language, on every channel including voice; a consent record per customer per restaurant carrying purpose, notice version, timestamp and channel. Built in from day one because retrofitting consent is not viable and the obligation lands on 13 May 2027. Consent captured at first order is a legal reading, not counsel-reviewed.

nodes.label: DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025
nodes.rationale: Rules notified 13 November 2025 with phased effect: Data Protection Board from November 2025, consent manager framework from November 2026, all remaining obligations from 13 May 2027. Penalties reach ₹250 crore. Covers phone numbers, names, addresses, dietary and allergy data, order history, payment behaviour and call recordings. Compliance is also used as a trust argument against aggregators who use customer data for themselves.

nodes.label: Single Tier at ₹4,999 per Month
nodes.rationale: One tier ships because only one tier is sellable before pilot data exists. A cheaper tier without the AI would be a weaker Petpooja at a price Petpooja beats and would route the most price-sensitive restaurants into the configuration containing none of the reasons ServeLine exists; a premium tier would contain inventory, loyalty and the seating optimiser, none of which exist. Three-tier packaging is a Phase 2 decision against real willingness-to-pay data.

nodes.label: 500 AI-Handled Calls with ₹5 Overage
nodes.rationale: An AI-handled call, for the allowance, is any inbound call the AI answers lasting longer than ten seconds; wrong numbers and instant hang-ups do not count. The metered allowance with overage is the guardrail against AI call COGS exceeding revenue at high-volume restaurants. The overage case is shown in the ROI table on purpose, because a restaurant discovering it mid-contract is a churn event.

nodes.label: 2% Fee on All ServeLine-Channel Orders
nodes.rationale: Decided 9 September 2026 to apply to every ServeLine-channel order — AI call, ordering page in either context, and win-back redemptions. The May draft said 'AI-assisted orders' and left it undefined, which would have made billing an argument. One rule is simpler to explain at onboarding, every ServeLine order runs on the AI-seeded menu and the profile, and the fee still charges nothing when no order happens.

nodes.label: Trial: 30 Days or 150 AI Calls
nodes.rationale: Whichever comes first. The agent visit happens inside this window and is the conversion moment; up to 150 trial calls of AI cost are carried inside CAC.

nodes.label: Cost per Call
nodes.rationale: ₹8 to ₹20 per three-minute call, central estimate ₹12, across telephony, STT (₹1.50/min at Sarvam September 2026 list, corrected up from an earlier ₹0.50-0.90), LLM turns and TTS. At 400 calls that is ₹4,800 against ₹4,999 of subscription — roughly zero gross margin before the transaction fee. The lever that fixes it is the customer database: a returning customer with history completes in one turn rather than ten, so cost per order falls as profile coverage rises and unit economics improve with time on the platform rather than degrading with volume.

nodes.label: Restaurant ROI Table
nodes.rationale: ₹1L monthly delivery revenue costs ₹28,000 in aggregator commission versus ₹6,999 on ServeLine within allowance, ₹7,999 at 700 calls. Both rows are shown because the flattering scenario alone is not a model. The win-back discount is presented at onboarding as funded by the commission the customer's later orders no longer pay, not as a discount the restaurant absorbs.

nodes.label: Acquisition Economics (CAC and Payback)
nodes.rationale: ₹10,000-12,000 per pilot restaurant (two to three loaded agent-days plus trial AI cost) against ₹2,000-3,000 monthly gross profit gives four-to-six-month payback and LTV/CAC around 4-5x at 5% monthly churn. Agent-led onboarding is a deliberate discovery cost with a stated exit condition.

nodes.label: AI Call Completion Rate
nodes.rationale: An inbound call with order intent ending in a confirmed order without human handoff, counted only if the order is not later corrected. Enquiry calls are excluded from the denominator. Without both conditions an AI that confidently mishears its way to a wrong order scores well. Staged 50% by week 4, 65% by week 8, 70% by week 12, because vocabulary seeding gets it working and real call recordings make it accurate — a flat 70% target assumes the system arrives finished.

nodes.label: Metric Guardrails
nodes.rationale: Restaurant monthly churn under 5%, onboarding under 3 days, AI call complaint rate under 1%, gross margin per restaurant positive by month 2, cost per call under ₹20 on a trailing seven-day average with an alert at ₹15. Cost per call is treated as a product guardrail, not an ops nicety.

nodes.label: Repeat-Order Shortcut ("Same as Last Time?")
nodes.rationale: Turns a three-minute call into a thirty-second one and is named the primary COGS lever; it is the mechanism by which a deeper profile directly lowers cost per order.

nodes.label: SMS Deflection for Enquiry Calls
nodes.rationale: Hours, address and menu questions are answered in one turn or the ordering page is sent by SMS, so enquiry traffic does not burn call minutes against the allowance.

nodes.label: Unconditional Call Forwarding to a Virtual Number
nodes.rationale: The restaurant keeps its existing number and forwards it. Nothing is ported, nothing is printed differently, and the restaurant can switch it off by dialling a code — the cost of trying ServeLine and the cost of leaving are both near zero.
nodes.norm_label: unconditional call forwarding to a virtual number

nodes.label: Carrier-Level Failover to the Owner's Mobile
nodes.rationale: If the AI service does not answer within three seconds the telephony flow itself routes the call to the owner's mobile. The failover deliberately lives in the carrier layer, not in ServeLine's application, so an outage at ServeLine degrades to today's behaviour rather than to a dead line.
nodes.norm_label: carrier-level failover to the owner's mobile

nodes.label: Hybrid Address Capture
nodes.rationale: Indian addresses do not survive a phone call intact. Returning customers get a saved address read back for a yes; new customers give area and landmark by voice, which is stored as a rough address with an immediate SMS link to complete on the page. The order sits in an address-pending state and the dashboard prompts a callback after five minutes. Delivery radius is checked by area and pincode before acceptance.

nodes.label: Restaurant-Owned Sub-Merchant Accounts
nodes.rationale: ServeLine never holds funds: each restaurant is its own sub-merchant on a licensed gateway, ServeLine only creates links and reads webhooks, and settlement goes straight to the restaurant. Collecting on the restaurant's behalf would make ServeLine a payment aggregator under RBI rules and require a licence the business cannot carry. ServeLine's own fees are a separate B2B invoice collected by UPI Autopay mandate.

nodes.label: Call Recording and Recording Notice
nodes.rationale: The accuracy loop depends on recordings, so the greeting carries a one-line recording notice in the detected language. Recordings are retained ninety days, scoped to the restaurant that received the call, and used only to tune that restaurant's vocabulary.

nodes.label: SMS DLT Registration
nodes.rationale: TRAI requires registration of the sending entity, sender headers and every template before transactional SMS can be delivered. It is a two-to-four-week lead item that starts before any code is written, which is why it is sequenced ahead of the codebase rather than treated as an integration task.

nodes.label: Menu Digitisation with AI Vocabulary Seeding
nodes.rationale: Explicitly not data entry: this is what sets speech recognition accuracy. Vocabulary seeding gets the AI working at onboarding; reinforcement from real call recordings makes it accurate. It is also the mitigation for dialect variation, rated medium severity and high likelihood.
nodes.norm_label: menu digitisation with ai vocabulary seeding

nodes.label: Agent-Led Onboarding
nodes.rationale: Agents digitise the menu, configure the AI, place the first cards and monitor the first fortnight of calls. They are also the research function — they see exactly where restaurants get stuck, which is what a self-serve flow needs to know before it can be built. It ends when CAC exceeds the cost of building self-serve, or at Phase 2.

nodes.label: Aggregator Commission Problem
nodes.rationale: Aggregators extract up to 30% per order from restaurants running 3 to 12% net margins; a restaurant putting 40% of revenue through Swiggy or Zomato at 28% commission loses an effective 10 to 12% of total revenue. The 'up to 30%' figure replaced an earlier '30 to 40%' that did not survive checking against published fee schedules.

nodes.label: Zomato
nodes.rationale: 58% of food delivery. Runs Zomato Base (free POS), Contactless Dining and Hyperpure at once, so it owns the delivery channel, the POS, dine-in ordering and ingredient supply simultaneously.

nodes.label: Swiggy
nodes.rationale: 34% of food delivery. Owns Dineout, inResto and Torqus, so it holds the delivery channel, reservations and the restaurant management system; also sells consumer ordering through ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

nodes.label: Petpooja
nodes.rationale: 50,000+ restaurants with POS, QR and an aggregator integration panel, and no AI ordering channel. It is the incumbent with distribution, and it already gives restaurants their customer data — which is why the data moat is rated weak.

nodes.label: DotPe
nodes.rationale: QR plus WhatsApp direct ordering with restaurant-owned customer data; cited alongside Petpooja as the reason there is no data moat.

nodes.label: TabSquare Aiden
nodes.rationale: AI-powered QR dine-in ordering with a claimed 25% AOV uplift; the closest conceptual competitor and the one product to watch, but enterprise-focused, not India-first, and with no call channel.

nodes.label: Horizontal Voice-Agent Platforms
nodes.rationale: Added September 2026, retiring the May sentence that nobody in India offered AI call ordering. Vyora, Vomyra, Ringg AI, MyOperator, Caller Digital and YuVerse sell Hindi and Kannada voice agents horizontally. None bundles a restaurant-owned ordering page, a win-back mechanism and a customer database, so the product white space holds — but build cost falls and the moat thins, because an incumbent POS can rent the same layer.

nodes.label: Structural Conflict of Interest (Strong Moat)
nodes.rationale: Zomato and Swiggy cannot hand customer ownership to restaurants without cannibalising the business that funds them. This is not a technology advantage and cannot be closed by shipping a feature; it is durable for as long as their economics depend on owning the customer, and it is why a well-funded aggregator will not simply copy the product.

nodes.label: Per-Restaurant AI Tuning (Moderate Moat)
nodes.rationale: Dish-name pronunciation, that kitchen's call patterns and the reinforcement signal from that restaurant's own recordings. A competitor starts from zero for every restaurant it wins. Worth months of lead, not years, and since the base voice layer is rentable the lead sits in the tuning data and the onboarding process, not the voice stack.

nodes.label: Customer Data Moat (Weak)
nodes.rationale: Rated weak on purpose. Petpooja and DotPe already give restaurants ownership of their data, and the advantage that does accrue belongs to the restaurant rather than to ServeLine — which is consistent with the positioning and would be dishonest to claim otherwise. The earlier claim 'twelve months of profiles is not copyable' is explicitly retired.

nodes.label: Incumbent POS Death Scenario
nodes.rationale: An incumbent POS with existing distribution rents a voice agent, ships an AI calling feature and reaches every target restaurant through a sales channel that already exists. Rated high severity and high likelihood, and more probable than an aggressive aggregator response. The counter is speed while incumbents treat AI as a feature rather than architecture, plus the observation that a platform serving 50,000 restaurants optimises for the average one.

nodes.label: MVP Scope
nodes.rationale: Ships the AI call assistant in three languages, the two-context ordering page, Direct Order Cards, phone-linked profiles, DPDP consent, menu digitisation, dashboard with weekly aggregator entry, UPI and COD, fallback and failover, agent-led onboarding and one ₹4,999 tier. Twelve named cuts (WhatsApp, upselling, recommendations, loyalty, inventory, KDS, SEO, self-serve, seating, vendor management, multi-location, extra languages) are all Phase 2 or 3.

nodes.label: MVP Exit Gate
nodes.rationale: Ten pilot restaurants onboarded in Bangalore, at least six reaching 30% Direct Order Share within 60 days, AI call completion at or above 70% by week 12, and positive gross margin per restaurant by month 2.

nodes.label: Phase 2: Expand the Channel
nodes.rationale: Months 6-12: WhatsApp ordering, loyalty, inventory, upselling and recommendations, self-serve onboarding informed by agent learnings, Tamil/Telugu/Bengali, tiered pricing against real willingness-to-pay data, SEO-indexed pages, and aggregator counts pulled by integration. Goal: 100+ restaurants at 40% median Direct Order Share.

nodes.label: Phase 3: Full Platform
nodes.rationale: Months 12-18: seating optimiser, kitchen display hardware, vendor management, enterprise tier with multi-location dashboards, Mumbai and Hyderabad. Goal: 500+ restaurants across three cities.

nodes.label: AI Fallback and Human Handoff
nodes.rationale: When AI confidence drops below threshold or the customer asks for a person, the call transfers, the incomplete order is flagged in the dashboard for staff to finish, and the partial profile is retained. It is both a trust signal and the guardrail on order accuracy.

nodes.label: Six-Minute Call Duration Cap
nodes.rationale: Overruns transfer to staff. This protects the cost tail without penalising the common case.

nodes.label: UPI
nodes.rationale: 228.3 billion transactions in 2025, 85.5% of digital payment volume, zero transaction cost against 1.5-2% for cards. Collecting payment for a direct order is free and instant, which removes the last operational reason to route through an aggregator — and a dominant zero-cost payment rail is one of the two conditions any future market must have.

nodes.label: Decision Log
nodes.rationale: Records what changed, what it replaced and why, with entries marked 'wrong' where an earlier draft asserted something that did not survive a second look — so a reader can tell a considered decision from an unexamined one.

nodes.label: Segment A: The Independent Restaurant (Primary ICP)
nodes.rationale: One to three owner-operated locations in Bangalore, 80-300 covers, ₹200-600 AOV, on Swiggy and Zomato at 18-30% commission with its own riders. Low tech comfort, which is why onboarding is agent-led. Pain is margin, brand and blindness. Every persona claim is flagged as an untested assumption.
nodes.norm_label: segment a: the independent restaurant (primary icp)

nodes.label: Customer Persona: The Regular
nodes.rationale: Urban, 25-40, Bangalore, orders from the same three to five restaurants roughly 80% of the time, WhatsApp-native and UPI-first. The regular is the entire economic case: a customer ordering twenty times a year from one restaurant is worth capturing once and keeping.

nodes.label: Parked: ServeLine Restaurant Directory
nodes.rationale: A cross-restaurant SEO-indexed marketplace was considered and rejected: ranking restaurants against each other creates exactly the conflict of interest ServeLine exists to attack, and the moment ServeLine controls placement it holds power over the restaurants paying it. It would also need two-sided liquidity a hundred Bangalore restaurants cannot supply, against a query class owned by Google Maps and the aggregators.

nodes.label: Per-Restaurant Indexed Pages
nodes.rationale: Accepted instead of a directory: each restaurant's own page ranking for its own branded searches. Branded queries are winnable because aggregators contest them with generic listing pages while the restaurant has the actual brand, and it intercepts the customer who searches the restaurant by name and lands on a Zomato listing. It needs no new surface — it is configuration on the Phase 1 ordering page.

nodes.label: Parked: International Expansion
nodes.rationale: Southeast Asia and the Middle East share the commission problem and nothing else that matters: the AI is tuned to Hindi/English/Kannada code-mixing, payments assume UPI at zero cost, messaging assumes WhatsApp at 89% of smartphone users, compliance is built to DPDP and unit economics assume Indian telephony and labour. Similar commission structures are the least transferable similarity. Reopens at 500 restaurants across three Indian cities retained past twelve months above 30% median Direct Order Share.

nodes.label: Assumptions Carried into MVP
nodes.rationale: No user research has been conducted, so every behavioural and persona claim is listed as an assumption with the test that would confirm or kill it — including pricing viability, the 40% call-to-order baseline, DPDP consent by opt-in, 8% win-back, reliable card placement, weekly count entry and mid-call address completion. The highest-value next action stated is five conversations with Bangalore restaurant owners before anything else is built.

nodes.label: Aggregator Partner Terms Risk
nodes.rationale: High severity, likelihood unknown, and the core mechanism sits on it: both partner agreements are unread. The card carries the restaurant's own brand, number and QR, which restaurants already print on packaging; if inserts are prohibited, the card moves to dine-in bills, takeaway bags and the restaurant's own rider deliveries, accepting a slower loop.

nodes.label: Voice Service (Pipecat, Python)
nodes.rationale: Python 3.12 and Pipecat self-hosted in Mumbai, chosen over renting Bolna because owning the pipeline is where per-restaurant tuning lives; Pipecat has a documented Exotel transport, and renting is the contingency only if M2 slips past three weeks. It is a client of the API with no database access, and is one of exactly two deployables.

nodes.label: Exotel
nodes.rationale: Chosen over Plivo, Knowlarity and Ozonetel for Indian carrier relationships, documented streaming and one vendor covering both voice and SMS; Twilio inbound in India is impractical. Provides virtual numbers, App Bazaar flows, the Voicebot applet, call transfer and recording.

nodes.label: Exotel AgentStream Bidirectional Streaming
nodes.rationale: 8 kHz 16-bit mono little-endian PCM, base64 in JSON frames over WebSocket; the voice service resamples to and from model rates. Whether transfer works while a stream is active is an open kickoff question that decides the handoff design.

nodes.label: Sarvam Bulbul v3 Text to Speech
nodes.rationale: Eleven Indian languages, Hinglish mid-sentence, low first-byte latency; ₹30 per 10,000 characters. Streamed by sentence to keep first-byte latency inside the budget.
nodes.norm_label: sarvam bulbul v3 text to speech

nodes.label: Razorpay Route
nodes.rationale: Route linked accounts per restaurant, Payment Links with UPI intent and 30-minute expiry, verified idempotent webhooks, and UPI Autopay mandates capped at ₹15,000 for ServeLine's own invoices. Chosen so the restaurant is merchant of record and ServeLine never holds funds.

nodes.label: LLM Vendor Adapter
nodes.rationale: Any tool-calling model with first token under 500 ms behind an adapter, with two providers wired from the start so a vendor outage is a config change rather than an incident. Phone numbers never enter a prompt, so residency exposure is limited to transcript text.

nodes.label: Next.js 15 Web and API
nodes.rationale: Chosen over a separate Fastify API: one deployable serving three UIs and the API means fewer moving parts for a small team.

nodes.label: Drizzle ORM and Migrations
nodes.rationale: Chosen over Prisma for plain SQL visibility, cheap migrations and good Postgres coverage.

nodes.label: Postgres 16 in Mumbai
nodes.rationale: Managed, branchable and in region, chosen over Supabase; everything stateful lives in Mumbai for DPDP residency.

nodes.label: Redis Session State and Queues
nodes.rationale: Chosen over Postgres-only queues for sub-10 ms session reads during a live call, plus BullMQ scheduled jobs for retention, billing and dashboard nags. Cart state during a call is owned by the API in Redis keyed by call id.

nodes.label: Postgres Data Model
nodes.rationale: Money in paise as integers, phone numbers in E.164 with a separate SHA-256 phone_hash, timestamps in UTC rendered Asia/Kolkata, soft deletes only where DPDP erasure does not apply. Customer profiles are per restaurant: customer is the platform identity and everything the restaurant knows hangs off customer_restaurant, so nothing crosses restaurants without new consent.

nodes.label: phone_hash (SHA-256 with Server Pepper)
nodes.rationale: Used for analytics and joins that do not need the number, so most of the system can key on a customer without ever holding a phone number.

nodes.label: consent_record Table
nodes.rationale: Stores customer, restaurant, notice_version, purposes, channel, language, granted_at, withdrawn_at and evidence (call id or request id and IP). Consent is required before any profile field beyond the phone number is stored; voice consent is the spoken yes after the notice, captured with the call id as evidence.

nodes.label: menu_vocabulary Table
nodes.rationale: Named as the speech accuracy lever: transliterations, nicknames and observed mishearings per item per language, with a source field distinguishing agent, ai and call_correction entries so the tuning loop is auditable.

nodes.label: external_order_count Table
nodes.rationale: Weekly Swiggy, Zomato and other order counts per outlet, unique on (outlet_id, week_start). Explicitly labelled the North Star denominator.

nodes.label: usage_ledger Table
nodes.rationale: Per-restaurant period record of AI calls, overage calls, channel order value, subscription, overage and fee, so an invoice can always be traced back to the counts that produced it.

nodes.label: card_batch, discount_code and code_redemption Tables
nodes.rationale: One redemption per phone per restaurant is enforced by a unique index on (code_id, customer_id) rather than by application logic, and card_batch carries printed_at, placed_at and placement_audited_at so redemption rate has a real denominator and a real start date.

nodes.label: audit_log Table
nodes.rationale: Actor, action, entity and before/after JSON for every write to customer data, so a DPDP access or erasure question can be answered with evidence rather than recollection.

nodes.label: dsar_request Table
nodes.rationale: Access, erasure and correction requests tracked to completion, because the Ideation file requires a deletion request path that works without engineering.

nodes.label: order Table and Status Machine
nodes.rationale: Channel (ai_call, page_table, page_delivery, staff_manual), fulfilment, payment and address status are separate axes, and the transitions include address_pending for voice orders with a rough address, awaiting_payment for UPI link orders and needs_attention for incomplete handoffs. correction_flag exists so a wrong order counts against call completion as well as against error rate.

nodes.label: customer_restaurant Table
nodes.rationale: Holds source, first_channel, consent_id, order_count, ltv_paise and usual_order per customer per restaurant — the per-restaurant tenancy boundary that makes 'the restaurant owns its customers' true in the schema, and the store for the repeat-order shortcut.

nodes.label: Voice Pipeline Guardrails
nodes.rationale: Confidence gating, menu grounding, a six-minute duration cap, silence handling, barge-in within 200 ms, instruction resistance (anything the customer says is data; the prompt and tools own prices and policy by construction), two abusive turns ends the call, and vendor_error transfer after two failures.

nodes.label: Menu Grounding
nodes.rationale: Menu search is a tool call, never free recall; every cart mutation must reference a menu id returned by search_menu in the same session and the API rejects anything else, so the model cannot invent an item or a price.

nodes.label: Turn Latency Budget
nodes.rationale: Transcript 300/500 ms, LLM first token 400/700 ms, TTS first byte 250/400 ms, whole turn 1.0 s p50 and 1.8 s p95; a short filler is played once per turn when a turn exceeds 1.2 s so silence never reads as a dropped call.

nodes.label: Prompt Architecture
nodes.rationale: Assembled per call from templates plus data and never hand-edited per restaurant, in a fixed order: persona and greeting rules, allowed languages, operating policies, the outlet card, the profile summary and the tool list. The profile summary deliberately excludes the phone number and the full address.

nodes.label: Voice LLM Tool Set
nodes.rationale: search_menu, add_to_cart, remove_from_cart, get_cart, apply_code, check_serviceability, use_saved_address, capture_rough_address, send_sms, place_order, answer_enquiry, transfer_to_human, end_call — JSON Schema served by the API, with every call logged on call_turn.tool_calls with arguments and result.

nodes.label: Voice Service to API Contract (Build Spec §5.6)
nodes.norm_label: voice service to api contract (build spec §5.6)

nodes.label: Post-STT Vocabulary Correction
nodes.rationale: The contingency if Sarvam does not accept a custom vocabulary: fuzzy-match transcript spans against the outlet's vocabulary (rapidfuzz, transliteration-aware) before the LLM sees the text, and log corrections for review. Designing both paths up front means the unanswered kickoff question does not block M4.

nodes.label: Ordering Page /r/{slug}
nodes.rationale: Server-rendered, under 100 KB of JavaScript, usable on a low-end Android over 3G, with no app or PWA install prompt — a link works where an app install does not. t={table} and c={code} select context; the address link /r/{slug}/address/{token} completes an address_pending order from a voice call.

nodes.label: Restaurant Dashboard
nodes.rationale: Mobile-first because it runs on the phone already at the counter. Live orders over Server-Sent Events with a 5-second polling fallback and an audible alert; needs_attention and address_pending orders pinned to the top; manual order entry for handoff calls; and a Monday aggregator count prompt that does not stop asking until it is answered.

nodes.label: Agent Console
nodes.rationale: Onboarding checklist, photo-to-menu extraction with an agent-corrected draft, vocabulary generation and review, and call review where a failure is tagged and an alias added in place with source = call_correction. This is where agent-led onboarding and the tuning loop actually live.

nodes.label: Phone OTP Authentication
nodes.rationale: OTP for everyone with JWT in httpOnly cookies, customer sessions 30 days and staff 7 days, chosen over passwords because nobody in this market wants a password.

nodes.label: Onboarding Checklist
nodes.rationale: Ten tracked steps ending in two weeks of monitored calls and the first weekly aggregator count. Step 4 requires the failover to be verified by pulling the voice service offline once — the safety net is tested during onboarding rather than assumed.

nodes.label: Metrics Instrumentation (SQL Views)
nodes.rationale: Every Ideation §9 metric maps to a named SQL view read by Metabase from a replica, with the definition written in data terms — for example completion counts only intent=order, answered_by=ai, outcome=completed calls whose linked order has correction_flag false.

nodes.label: Monthly Billing and Metering Job
nodes.rationale: ₹4,999 subscription, ₹5 per allowance call beyond 500, and 2% of total_paise on ServeLine-channel orders that reached delivered or completed dine-in, with cancelled orders excluded. Debited by mandate with a payment link on failure and a dashboard banner after 3 days. At the trial limit the Exotel flow reverts to dialling the owner mobile and the ordering page stays live — nothing is deleted.

nodes.label: Nightly Retention Jobs
nodes.rationale: Recordings deleted at 90 days; transcripts anonymised at 12 months with the customer id removed but the text kept for tuning; orders kept as long as tax law requires; OTPs 10 minutes. Retention is a scheduled job rather than a policy document, so the limit is enforced by default.

nodes.label: Erasure Workflow
nodes.rationale: Deletes profile, addresses, preferences, consent and call transcripts for that restaurant (or platform-wide), and nulls customer_id on orders while keeping the order for accounting — reconciling DPDP erasure with tax retention. Completed within 7 days and logged.

nodes.label: Voice Evaluation Harness
nodes.rationale: From M2 and growing every milestone: at least 200 scripted utterances per outlet menu per language, recorded by five speakers over a real phone line with kitchen noise, run against staging on every voice change. Targets item accuracy 85% at M2, 92% at M3, 95% after vocabulary tuning at M4.

nodes.label: Questions to Settle at Kickoff
nodes.rationale: Six unresolved vendor and legal questions are listed with the decision each one unblocks — Sarvam custom vocabulary, Exotel mid-stream transfer and streaming price, Razorpay Route KYC turnaround, DLT lead time, counsel's view on offshore inference and spoken consent, and whether pilot carriers allow unconditional forwarding. Naming them keeps unknowns out of the milestone plan.

nodes.label: Milestones and Acceptance Criteria
nodes.rationale: Seven milestones over eighteen weeks, each ending with a demo on a real phone and each defined by acceptance criteria written as tests — a milestone is done when they pass, not when the code exists.

nodes.label: M0: Foundations
nodes.rationale: Weeks 1-2: monorepo, CI, environments, Mumbai Postgres and Redis, S3, OTP auth, tenancy and menu tables, a three-language Bangalore seed, and vendor accounts opened with the DLT application filed. Done when a staff user logs in by OTP on staging, migrations run from zero and the DLT reference number is recorded.

nodes.label: M1: Orders Without AI
nodes.rationale: Weeks 3-5: both ordering page contexts, dashboard, manual entry, menu editor, card batches and codes, Razorpay linked accounts and payment links, SMS (stubbed until DLT approves), consent records and aggregator count entry. Done when a real phone pays by UPI into the restaurant's own account, a second redemption by the same phone is refused, and the Monday prompt persists until answered.

nodes.label: M2: Voice v0
nodes.rationale: Weeks 6-9: Exotel transport, Sarvam STT/TTS, two-provider LLM adapter, tools, session init and cart via the API, read-back, order placement, SMS payment link, transfer, verified carrier failover, recordings, turn logging and the cost ledger. Hindi and English only. Done when a forwarded call from a real mobile places a three-item order in Hindi, handoff works, the service being stopped rings the owner mobile, and p95 turn latency over 20 calls is under 1.8 s.

nodes.label: M3: Voice v1
nodes.rationale: Weeks 10-12: Kannada and code-mixing, repeat-order shortcut, enquiry answering and SMS deflection, hybrid address capture with address_pending, serviceability, duration cap, silence and confidence handling, abuse handling and usual_order refresh. Done when a returning customer completes in under 40 seconds via 'same as last time' and a 7-minute call transfers at 6 minutes.

nodes.label: M4: Menu Digitisation and the Tuning Loop
nodes.rationale: Weeks 13-14: agent console checklist, photo-to-menu extraction and editor, vocabulary generation, vocabulary push or post-STT correction depending on Sarvam's answer, and call review with in-place alias creation. Done when an agent turns three menu photos into a published menu with vocabulary in under 45 minutes, and a deliberately mispronounced item is misheard, tagged, aliased and recognised on the next call.
nodes.norm_label: m4: menu digitisation and the tuning loop

nodes.label: M5: Compliance, Billing and Metrics
nodes.rationale: Weeks 15-16: retention jobs, erasure, audit coverage, versioned notices in three languages, breach runbook, usage ledger, invoices, mandates, trial limits, Metabase views and cost alerts. Done when an erasure removes a test customer everywhere except anonymised orders in one job run and a month-end job matches a hand calculation (620 calls, ₹80,000 channel orders: ₹4,999 + ₹600 + ₹1,600).

nodes.label: M6: Pilot Readiness
nodes.rationale: Weeks 17-18: three Bangalore restaurants live, ops runbooks, on-call rota, agent daily review routine and a weekly pilot report. Done when three real restaurants have taken real paid orders through both call and page for seven consecutive days with no P1 open.

nodes.label: Build Spec Repository Layout (apps/services/packages)
nodes.rationale: A monorepo of apps/web, services/voice, packages/db and packages/shared, with docs for vendors, runbooks and ADRs — proposed because TypeScript and Python must coexist and the contract between them is small and versioned.

nodes.label: Consent Notices Contract
nodes.rationale: The text a customer agrees to before ServeLine stores anything beyond their phone number. One directory per version, one file per language (hi, en, kn). The directory name is the exact value stored in consent_record.notice_version, so v1/ and the string v1 must never drift apart. Markdown rather than TypeScript because the Python voice service reads these same files and speaks the notice aloud.

nodes.label: Notice Immutability Rule
nodes.source_location: Never edit a notice in place
nodes.rationale: A consent record stores a pointer, not the words the customer read. Change the words behind the pointer and every existing record claims agreement to something the customer never saw, with nothing in the data able to say which text they actually agreed to — and consent you cannot evidence is, under the DPDP Act, consent you do not have. The rule is deliberately mechanical with no judgement call at the keyboard, because you cannot tell from inside the code whether a typo changed the meaning: a missing 'not' is a typo, so is '90 days' where '12 months' was meant. Fix a typo by cutting v2; it costs one directory. The only permitted edit is to a version never released and never referenced by a consent_record.

nodes.label: Spoken Rendering of a Notice
nodes.rationale: Both renderings are v1 because both describe the same handling of the same data, so a consent_record pointing at v1 is honest whichever one the customer got. The spoken version is shorter on purpose: nobody listens to two hundred and fifty words on the phone, and a notice nobody listens to is not consent. It covers order_fulfilment and order_history only, so a call consent grants less than a page consent; call_recording belongs to the telephone transport's own greeting notice, and the browser transport records nothing. A rendering is immutable exactly like the notice it renders.

nodes.label: Consent Purpose Keys
nodes.rationale: order_fulfilment, order_history, personalisation and call_recording. The notice's purposes are what the version covers; consent_record.purposes is what a given customer actually granted, which may be a subset — a page order grants no call_recording because no call happened. A purpose absent from the version the customer signed is not granted no matter what the record says. Adding a purpose key to an existing version is a change of meaning and needs a new directory.

nodes.label: {{restaurant_name}} Placeholder
nodes.rationale: The only placeholder, and deliberately the only one: the restaurant is the data fiduciary and ServeLine its processor, so the notice must name the restaurant. It is substituted at render on the page and before text-to-speech on a call, and every additional placeholder is another thing the voice service must know how to fill.

nodes.label: Notice Frontmatter Schema
nodes.rationale: version matching the directory name, language matching the hi|en|kn enum, effective_date, and the purposes the version covers — machine-readable so the version/directory agreement and the purpose coverage check can both be enforced in code.

nodes.label: src/core/consent.ts
nodes.rationale: Answers 'is this purpose covered, under the version this customer agreed to' — the check that makes the notice's purpose list, not the consent record alone, the ceiling on what may be done with a customer's data.

nodes.label: ADR 0001
nodes.rationale: Cited as the decision that notices live as Markdown in contracts/ rather than in TypeScript, because the Python voice service reads them at M2.

nodes.label: ADR 0002
nodes.rationale: Cited (§4) as recording that the Hindi and Kannada renderings are interim translations.

nodes.label: Consent Notice v1 (English, Read)
nodes.rationale: Covers all four purposes. States what is collected, why, retention (recordings 90 days, transcripts 12 months then de-identified, order records as tax law requires), that only the restaurant and its staff see it and it is never shared with other ServeLine restaurants or sold, that ordering from another ServeLine restaurant needs fresh consent, and that withdrawal or deletion is one tap or a word to the restaurant, completed within 7 days with past bills kept without the name.

nodes.label: Data Protection Board of India
nodes.rationale: Named in the notice as the escalation route after the restaurant; it is the body the DPDP Rules brought into effect from November 2025.

nodes.label: Consent Notice v1 (Hindi, Read)
nodes.rationale: Same four purposes and same effective date as the English notice; flagged as an interim translation not reviewed by counsel.

nodes.label: Consent Notice v1 (Kannada, Read)
nodes.rationale: Same four purposes and same effective date as the English notice; flagged as an interim translation not reviewed by counsel.

nodes.label: Spoken Consent Notice v1 (English)
nodes.rationale: Four sentences covering order_fulfilment and order_history only: who keeps what, why, that it goes nowhere else, that it can be deleted, where the full text is, and a closing 'Is that alright?' whose yes is the captured consent.

nodes.label: Spoken Consent Notice v1 (Hindi)
nodes.rationale: Hindi rendering of the spoken notice; same two purposes, ends in a yes/no question suitable for a phone call.

nodes.label: Spoken Consent Notice v1 (Kannada)
nodes.rationale: Kannada rendering of the spoken notice; same two purposes, ends in a yes/no question suitable for a phone call.

nodes.label: Voice Evaluation Set
nodes.rationale: Build Spec §16's scripted utterance set per language, measuring item recognition accuracy, intent accuracy and turn latency. Every case runs as its own call against the seeded demo menu so cases never interfere.

nodes.label: Evaluation Case Shape
nodes.rationale: say is one caller utterance as spoken, code-mixed where a caller would code-mix; intent is order, enquiry or other; expect.items is the cart afterwards with names exactly as the menu spells them, an empty list being the correct outcome for an enquiry; expect.tool names the tool that must have been called and succeeded where the outcome is not a cart (answer_enquiry, transfer_to_human, check_serviceability, apply_code).

nodes.label: Item Recognition Accuracy
nodes.rationale: The fraction of cart cases whose cart matched exactly — the §16 target, defined as the item that ends up in the cart being the item spoken, not a transcription score.

nodes.label: Intent Accuracy
nodes.rationale: The fraction of cases classified correctly. Errored cases (rate limit, outage) are excluded from both measures, and a run with many of them is explicitly not a measurement.

nodes.label: Text-only baseline, 23 September 2026 — 100% item accuracy in all three languages
nodes.rationale: Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite (ADR 0006), 90 cases, after the prompt fix. English 100% (20/20) item, 100% (27/27) intent, p50 4.3 s, p95 6.5 s, 3 errored. Hindi 100% (29/29), p50 4.9 s, p95 8.4 s, 1 errored. Kannada 100% (30/30), p50 5.5 s, p95 9.4 s, 0 errored. Zero genuine failures. Kannada ran its full thirty with no rate-limit errors at all, so that column is a complete sample rather than a flattered one — which matters, because the previous run recorded 86% there over only 22 scored cases. 4 of 90 errored on a rate limit even at --gap 6000; this is the free tier.
nodes.norm_label: text-only baseline, 23 september 2026 — 100% item accuracy in all three languages

nodes.label: Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite
nodes.rationale: The provider behind the baseline run, selected per ADR 0006; run on a free-tier key, which is why a fifth of the set hit a rate limit.

nodes.label: ADR 0006
nodes.rationale: Cited as the decision selecting Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite as the evaluated LLM provider.

nodes.label: ADR 0001 — A single application instead of the Build Spec's monorepo
nodes.rationale: Accepted 18 Sep 2026; supersedes Build Spec §15. At M1 there is one deployable (the Next.js app, which is also the API); the voice service does not exist until M2 and is Python, reaching the app over HTTP (§5.6), so it can never import TypeScript. A workspace tool would manage a single package, and the one genuine cross-language artefact (tool JSON Schemas, consent notice texts) is plain data both languages read from disk. Modularity is carried by internal module boundaries enforced by a lint rule rather than directory ceremony, so it is checked rather than assumed. Reversal cost is low: extracting src/core into a package is a directory move.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0001 — a single application instead of the build spec's monorepo

nodes.label: ADR 0002 — Resolving the design language's open decisions
nodes.norm_label: adr 0002 — resolving the design language's open decisions

nodes.label: ADR 0003 — The ordering page's JavaScript budget
nodes.norm_label: adr 0003 — the ordering page's javascript budget

nodes.label: ADR 0004 — The voice assistant's brain lives in the API, in TypeScript
nodes.rationale: Amends Build Spec §3 and §15. At M2 there is no telephone line and no speech vendor; what can be built is the conversation — prompt, model, fourteen tools, guardrails, ledger — all of which depends on src/core and the repositories, which are TypeScript, and none of which touches audio. Keeping the brain in-process means the assistant runs the same priceCart and the same placeOrder as the web page by import rather than by HTTP, so pricing cannot drift between channels, and the whole conversation is unit-testable with a mock model. The cost is latency on a transport-to-API hop, mitigated by co-locating the transport in Mumbai.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0004 — the voice assistant's brain lives in the api, in typescript

nodes.label: ADR 0005 — Spoken consent, and a fourteenth tool
nodes.rationale: Extends Build Spec §5.5, implements §10. The M2 review found place_order writing a customer_restaurant profile row for a caller who had never agreed to anything; the consent gate went in and then made the assistant useless to the stranger phoning a restaurant, which Ideation §7 calls the wedge. §5.5's thirteen tools contain no way to record a spoken yes, so a fourteenth tool was added. The prompt is the manners, the gate is the guarantee. Counsel has not reviewed the shortened spoken rendering; two questions are flagged for that review.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0005 — spoken consent, and a fourteenth tool

nodes.label: ADR 0006 — Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite, chosen by measurement
nodes.norm_label: adr 0006 — gemini 3.5 flash lite, chosen by measurement

nodes.label: ADR 0007 — Local models: measured, and what they are good for
nodes.norm_label: adr 0007 — local models: measured, and what they are good for

nodes.label: src/core — domain logic with no framework imports
nodes.rationale: Cart pricing, the order state machine, code redemption, serviceability and consent gating as pure functions over plain data, importing neither next nor react nor the database. The boundary is enforced by a lint rule, not by convention. This is the layer the voice tool calls reuse at M2, and it is what stops the AI quoting a different price from the web page.
nodes.norm_label: src/core — domain logic with no framework imports

nodes.label: src/db — Drizzle schema, migrations, seed, repositories
nodes.rationale: Every write to customer data goes through a repository function that also writes the audit log, so auditing is a property of the layer rather than of each call site.
nodes.norm_label: src/db — drizzle schema, migrations, seed, repositories

nodes.label: src/adapters — one folder per vendor concern
nodes.rationale: Interface plus working mock per vendor, so the product runs end to end with no vendor account. A live account later is a new implementation of the same interface selected by an environment variable, never a change to calling code. This is not a shortcut around the vendors but around waiting for them — DLT template approval alone is a two-to-four week external dependency.
nodes.norm_label: src/adapters — one folder per vendor concern

nodes.label: src/ui — design tokens and shared components
nodes.rationale: Tokens are CSS custom properties; a colour or spacing value is never hard-coded in a component.
nodes.norm_label: src/ui — design tokens and shared components

nodes.label: src/voice — the call assistant's brain
nodes.rationale: prompt.ts assembles the system prompt, tools.ts holds the fourteen handlers thin over src/core and src/db/repos, loop.ts runs one turn with guardrails and the ledger, session.ts holds per-call state in memory keyed by call id. Never imports next; called by the route handlers and by tests, so the future Python transport and the browser are indistinguishable to it.

nodes.label: contracts/ — language-neutral JSON and Markdown
nodes.rationale: Plain data read by TypeScript now and by Python at M2. This is the one genuine cross-language artefact, and because it is data on disk rather than a shared package it removes the only reason the Build Spec's monorepo existed.

nodes.label: app/ — routes only, kept thin
nodes.rationale: Business rules belong in src/core; validation sits at the trust boundary so core functions may assume well-formed data.

nodes.label: npm rather than pnpm
nodes.rationale: corepack prepare pnpm@latest fails on this machine with a broken module cache. With no workspaces to manage, npm is sufficient, so the repo does not spend time on the corepack fault. Revisit if workspaces ever return.

nodes.label: Lint-enforced core boundary
nodes.rationale: The boundary that actually matters — domain logic separated from delivery mechanism — is enforced by a lint rule rather than by directory ceremony, which means it is checked rather than assumed.

nodes.label: WCAG 2.2 AA as the accessibility standard
nodes.rationale: Settled because the design's every contrast pair was already computed against it, nothing in the Ideation file asks for more, and the audience — low-end Android, low tech comfort, three scripts — is exactly who AA protects.
nodes.norm_label: wcag 2.2 aa as the accessibility standard

nodes.label: Dark mode: customer follows the OS, dashboard has a manual toggle
nodes.rationale: The design's own recommendation, adopted. A restaurant's brand colour is normalised for both themes so the customer page is safe either way; a counter is bright at noon and dim at 11pm and the operator knows which they want better than the OS does.
nodes.norm_label: dark mode: customer follows the os, dashboard has a manual toggle

nodes.label: Order-state labels in Hindi and Kannada — interim, flagged for native review
nodes.rationale: No native speaker is on the team, so six labels ship with a reviewed:false flag per language and the dashboard shows them. Ready is the safety-critical one and has no single obvious equivalent in either language. Pending: a native speaker reviews before the first pilot restaurant is live.
nodes.norm_label: order-state labels in hindi and kannada — interim, flagged for native review

nodes.label: Alert sound deferred until a real kitchen
nodes.rationale: Specify after testing, not before. M1 ships a placeholder two-tone chime behind the same tap-to-enable-sounds gesture the design specifies, so the audio-unlock flow is built and tested even though the sound itself will change.
nodes.norm_label: alert sound deferred until a real kitchen

nodes.label: Delivered for dine-in: one state, two labels
nodes.rationale: Build Spec §4 has a single terminal success state and §12's metric treats delivered and dine-in completed as one, so the state stays one and only the UI label differs by fulfilment — Delivered, Served, Collected. A label is not a state; adding an enum member for a wording difference would be scaffolding.
nodes.norm_label: delivered for dine-in: one state, two labels

nodes.label: Lighthouse mobile performance ≥ 85 as the ordering page's budget
nodes.rationale: Replaces Build Spec §6's byte figure with the outcome it stood for, measured on the production build on every change to the customer surface. Current baseline 99; a change dropping it below 90 needs a reason. Server rendering means the menu, prices and category navigation paint before any script arrives, and zero webfonts with no images by default are what keep byte weight and LCP where they are.
nodes.norm_label: lighthouse mobile performance ≥ 85 as the ordering page's budget

nodes.label: Non-framework JavaScript under 40 KB gzipped
nodes.rationale: A secondary guard so the app's own contribution does not creep while the framework floor is uncontrollable; today about 30 KB. The i18n dictionary, 8 KB carrying all three languages, is the first thing to split per language if the line is approached.

nodes.label: The React 19 + App Router framework floor
nodes.rationale: react-dom 69 KB plus 71 KB of Next.js client runtime is roughly 140 KB gzipped before a line of ServeLine code runs, which is why the 100 KB budget cannot be met on this stack by any amount of trimming.
nodes.norm_label: the react 19 + app router framework floor

nodes.label: Escape hatch: serve /r/{slug} from something lighter than the App Router
nodes.rationale: If a real pilot on real handsets in a real Bangalore kitchen shows the customer surface failing, one surface is rewritten as a server-rendered page with a few hundred lines of plain JavaScript for the cart. src/core, the repositories and the API are unchanged by it. Do not take it pre-emptively; the numbers say it is not needed.
nodes.norm_label: escape hatch: serve /r/{slug} from something lighter than the app router

nodes.label: contracts/voice-tools.json — the tool JSON Schemas
nodes.rationale: Language-neutral by design and never inlined, read by the TypeScript handlers, the tests and the future Python transport. Fourteen tools: §5.5's thirteen plus record_consent.

nodes.label: /api/v1/voice/* — session-init, turn, tools/{name}, end
nodes.rationale: The Build Spec §5.6 contract. Two transports talk to it: the browser today and a Python/Pipecat process when an Exotel number exists. Nothing in src/voice knows which.

nodes.label: Python/Pipecat telephone transport
nodes.rationale: Deferred to M2b, when an Exotel number and Sarvam speech exist. It is a thin client of the same API; on reversal it could absorb the loop by importing the same tool contract, leaving src/voice as the tool handlers, which is where the value is anyway.

nodes.label: Build Spec §5.4 turn latency budget
nodes.rationale: 400 ms to the model's first token, 1.0 s p50 and 1.8 s p95 for a whole turn. It is the number that decided the model choice in ADR 0006 and that ruled out local models in ADR 0007.

nodes.label: record_consent(agreed: boolean) — the fourteenth tool
nodes.rationale: Writes a consent_record with channel call, the notice version in force, and evidence of callId, transport and rendering spoken. A departure from §5.5's list of thirteen; anyone comparing the two should read ADR 0005.

nodes.label: Spoken rendering of the consent notice
nodes.rationale: About sixty words against the read notice's two hundred and fifty, carrying the same version because it describes the same handling of the same data, so a consent_record pointing at v1 is honest whichever rendering the customer got. Fewer purposes: spoken words cover order_fulfilment and order_history only, so a call consent grants less than a page consent. call_recording belongs to the telephone transport's own greeting; the browser transport records nothing.
nodes.norm_label: spoken rendering of the consent notice

nodes.label: place_order refuses consent_required until consent is recorded
nodes.rationale: The prompt carries the notice only for a caller without live consent and instructs the assistant to read it word for word before placing anything, but the prompt is the manners and the gate is the guarantee. A caller who says no is offered the ordering page by SMS; a handoff before consent parks no order. An anonymous call still cannot place an order because there is no identity to attach consent or an order to.
nodes.norm_label: place_order refuses consent_required until consent is recorded

nodes.label: Counsel has not reviewed the spoken rendering
nodes.rationale: Ideation §15 already flags the consent approach as a legal reading rather than counsel-reviewed and this sits inside that gap. Two specific questions: whether a shortened spoken rendering may carry the same version as the read notice, and whether a recorded spoken yes is sufficient evidence under the DPDP Rules.
nodes.norm_label: counsel has not reviewed the spoken rendering

nodes.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite as the primary model
nodes.rationale: Pinned rather than aliased, overridable by GEMINI_MODEL so the next retirement is a configuration change. Median 1.19 s and worst 1.57 s over five runs, inside the 1.8 s budget; flash-lite-latest had a marginally better median but a 9.8 s outlier and a floating alias can change behaviour without a deploy. The model is a tier below what §3 assumed and on a harder call may do worse; the cure is measurement, not a bigger model.

nodes.label: thinkingConfig thinkingLevel low
nodes.rationale: Low and not off because thinkingBudget 0 is rejected with a 400 by this model, and low still reads a three-dish code-mixed order correctly. A caller on a phone cannot wait for deliberation, which is the same reason the local adapter sets think:false.

nodes.label: Gemini model latency measurement, 21 September 2026
nodes.rationale: One tool, a three-dish Hinglish order, five runs each. Every model produced the correct three search_menu calls, so the distinguishing fact is time: full Flash models ran 5.7-120 s or returned 503. The 503s may be this key's quota rather than the models, so re-run against a pilot key.

nodes.label: contracts/voice-eval — the voice evaluation harness seed
nodes.rationale: Thirty caller utterances per language with expected tool calls, run against the mock now and the real model when a key exists. It is what should decide whether the lite tier holds, on real utterances, before a pilot.
nodes.norm_label: contracts/voice-eval — the voice evaluation harness seed

nodes.label: src/voice/pricing.ts — token prices in paise
nodes.rationale: Dated list prices per million tokens with a comment to re-check. The lite tier's list price was not reachable and is recorded as unverified — check it at kickoff. Cost falls to roughly a third of the 2.5 Flash line, so Ideation §10's ₹8-20 per call estimate still holds with room to spare.

nodes.label: Local model measurement on an M2 Pro MacBook Pro, 22 September 2026
nodes.rationale: Identical work in every case: the same three-turn Hindi order through src/voice/loop.ts against the same fourteen tools and the same prompt, with failovers discarded so a mock answering in microseconds cannot flatter a result. Hosted Flash Lite 2.9 s p50 and completed the flow; Qwen3 8B 15.7 s and never reached the order.
nodes.norm_label: local model measurement on an m2 pro macbook pro, 22 september 2026

nodes.label: Qwen3 8B and 14B run locally
nodes.rationale: Bigger is worse here: 14B is twice as slow as 8B and less accurate, dropping a dish from a two-dish order, and on 16 GB there is nothing above 14B to try, so a stronger local model is not an available answer. Thinking is most of the cost — 53 s a turn becomes 15.7 s with think:false. A turn is two to four sequential model calls over a prompt of fourteen tool schemas, and prompt processing is what a laptop is slow at.

nodes.label: whisper.cpp large-v3-turbo as the intended speech-to-text for M2b
nodes.rationale: q5_0, 547 MB, run as a persistent server: about 1.9 s warm per clip, 22 s cold start that is irrelevant to a server that stays up. Accurate on both languages tested. This is the piece worth having because it substitutes for the Sarvam dependency that cannot be bought yet and runs on the restaurant's own machine. Not wired yet — replacing the browser recogniser is transport work belonging with the Exotel audio path.
nodes.norm_label: whisper.cpp large-v3-turbo as the intended speech-to-text for m2b

nodes.label: src/adapters/llm/ollama.ts — a kept but non-default provider
nodes.rationale: Selected by LLM_PRIMARY_PROVIDER=ollama with OLLAMA_MODEL and OLLAMA_HOST. Kept because it costs nothing to keep, it is the offline demo when no network is available, and the measurement table is worth being able to re-run on better hardware. Not the default and should not be until a measurement says otherwise.
nodes.norm_label: src/adapters/llm/ollama.ts — a kept but non-default provider

nodes.label: Indic text-to-speech locally is the weak link
nodes.rationale: Not pursued: Piper's Hindi voices are below Bulbul's and Kannada barely exists. The browser's own voices, which /r/{slug}/call already uses, run on the device anyway.
nodes.norm_label: indic text-to-speech locally is the weak link

nodes.label: consent_record — the DPDP consent row
nodes.rationale: Written before any customer field beyond the phone number is stored, and never edited in place — a change of notice text means a new version. Carries the channel (page or call), the notice version in force, and the evidence; for a call that evidence is the call id, the transport and the rendering. It is what place_order's gate reads, and what a consent recorded without an answer falsely creates.

nodes.label: order-number-day-boundary-tz (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: Counter board order numbers restart at #1 at 7pm, mid dinner service, because the +330 minute IST shift stacks on a PGlite session TimeZone of Etc/GMT-5, giving an effective UTC+10:30. Two live orders both show #1 and staff hand the wrong bag to the wrong customer; the Done group is cut at true IST midnight so the list and the numbering disagree about what today is. Fix: pin the bucket expression to UTC so it cannot depend on the session TimeZone.

nodes.label: voice-place-order-not-idempotent (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: One phone call produces two identical orders: the kitchen cooks twice, the caller gets four SMS including two live payment links, and the call row records only the second order id so the first duplicate is invisible from the review screen. Any real model that re-issues the tool after a timeout or a repeated caller confirmation triggers it. Fix requires both layers — a session guard and a database-level guard — not the session guard alone.

nodes.label: place-order-not-idempotent-per-call (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: Found independently by a second hunter. A caller who changes their mind after the assistant has already placed the order gets two real orders; call.order_id points only at the second, so the first is orphaned from the call that made it. On a paid channel this is a double charge.

nodes.label: consent-recorded-without-an-answer (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: session.noticeRead is set from response.text before the same response's tool calls run, so one model response can both read the notice aloud and call record_consent{agreed:true}; the caller never gets a turn in which to answer. A DPDP consent_record is written for a caller who was never asked, and the transcript proves they never said yes; the record then unlocks place_order so a profile row is written too. ADR 0005's gate does not survive a model that batches text with a tool call, which Gemini routinely does. Fix: require the notice to have gone out in a strictly earlier turn — state.seq is not reachable from a tool handler, so the claimed mechanics were wrong even though the shape was right.

nodes.label: direct-order-share-divides-month-by-partial-weeks (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: The North Star is computed over mismatched spans — a whole month of delivered orders over only those aggregator weeks whose Monday falls inside that month — so it is systematically overstated and reads 100% for roughly the first week of every month even when half the orders come from aggregators, because no Monday has fallen yet and the denominator is zero. share() only returns null when both are zero, so the needs-last-week's-counts hint never fires. A pilot restaurant would be scored against Ideation §9's 30% target on a number that cannot be right. Fix belongs in the repo layer, not the page.

nodes.label: refused-code-blocks-order (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: Once a discount code in the URL is refused, placeOrder returns code_refused instead of pricing without the discount, so no order can ever be placed from that URL and the retry path re-sends the same code forever. This kills the exact win-back loop the business rests on: a returning customer rescanning their Direct Order Card taps Place order and nothing happens, ever, and the restaurant never learns it was lost. Build Spec §6 says the opposite. Fix on the caller side, not in placeOrder — the server-side refusal is deliberately asserted by a test and protects a lost-race cancellation.

nodes.label: unpriceable-cart-line-kills-cart (HIGH, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: An ordinary menu edit — making an option group required, or lowering a maximum — leaves saved cart lines that violate minSelect/maxSelect, which prune does not check. priceCart throws, both callers swallow the throw into cart = null, and the customer sees their dishes listed with quantities, no cart bar, no error and no way to checkout; the cart is never cleared so the trap persists. Fix: make prune the single authority on whether a line can still be priced, make the drop visible, and never render items with no cart bar.

nodes.label: order-confirm-sms-claims-unpaid-order-is-paid (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: The customer's phone receives two contradictory messages within a second: order received, paid by UPI, and pay Rs 90 by UPI. A diner who reads the first stops, never pays, and turns up at the counter believing the order is settled. Fix: forward-looking wording that names the mode without asserting payment, kept ASCII so the GSM-7 segment cost is unchanged.

nodes.label: superseded-payment-link-still-payable (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: attachPayment's own comment claims the link it replaces is closed; nothing closes it. A customer tapping both SMS links pays twice, one row is paid and the other sits at awaiting with no payment id, no amount and no payload, so there is no trace of the second capture anywhere and nothing to refund against. The misleading comment is what makes this look fixed on a read-through. The cancel must not go inside attachPayment, which runs in a transaction in the database layer — a vendor HTTP call there both breaks the layering and holds a transaction open across the network.

nodes.label: address-pending-order-never-confirmed-by-sms (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: A caller who ordered by phone paying cash gets no written record at all of what they ordered or what it costs — the items and total exist only on a status page they happened to be redirected to. This is the customer who could not read a menu, which is why they phoned.

nodes.label: cod-conversion-leaves-upi-link-live (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: The counter takes cash because the UPI payment has not landed, and the payment-link SMS stays live for the rest of its 30 minutes; the moment the customer taps it the gateway captures again and the order flips to Paid, so nobody at the restaurant can tell which payment actually happened. Database bookkeeping alone does not stop a capture — the gateway-side cancel is what closes the hole.

nodes.label: trial-invoice-charges-subscription (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: A restaurant in its free trial reads Free trial — 30 days left on the same screen as an estimated invoice of ₹5,005.30 including a ₹4,999 subscription line it does not owe, and an allowance of 0/500 when the trial limit is 150. restaurant.trialCallLimit is in scope two lines above the constant that was used instead. Every pilot restaurant starts here.

nodes.label: negative-unit-price-cart (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: An owner publishing a variant or option delta larger than the base price creates orders with negative totals: a negative bill on the ticket and status page, no UPI link because the total is not positive, a reduced platform fee, and with a code applied a RangeError that is not a CartError and so escapes every catch, reaching the customer as Something went wrong. It also quietly undercharges when one negative line sits inside an otherwise positive cart, because that cart never reaches the discount path at all. Needs an owner to publish the row, so no customer can trigger it unaided — but once published it is money-wrong. The guard belongs on the accumulated unit price and in the repository choke point, not only in the two form parsers.

nodes.label: read-back-total-is-not-the-charged-total (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: The assistant reads back ₹240, the caller says yes, and the order is created at ₹400, because the read-back prices a snapshot while placeOrder prices the live menu. Nobody is told the price moved. The trigger is an ordinary counter action — editing a dish's price during service — while a call is in flight. Treated as the top medium because the money impact is unbounded. Pricing against the live menu introduces a new throw path that must be caught, or a dish toggled sold out mid-call kills the call instead of being explained to the caller.

nodes.label: call-cost-misses-the-sms-the-call-sent (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: Only the send_sms tool adds to the ledger, so the SMS placeOrder sends from inside itself are logged with their cost but never reach call_cost. Every call that actually places an order under-reports its own cost, and the cost column is wrong for exactly the calls that matter most — the successful ones. Build Spec §12's per-call thresholds are read off this number, so the alarm is calibrated against a figure that is systematically low.

nodes.label: resend-payment-link-on-terminal-order (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: A second counter phone whose board has not caught up sends a live pay-now SMS for an order the restaurant has cancelled; the webhook then records the payment against the cancelled order, so the customer has paid for food they will not get and nothing on the board flags it for refund. The card already carries the isTerminal check, so the only guard is the client.

nodes.label: closing-short-circuits-tool-bookkeeping (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: A logical-assignment short-circuit means note() is not evaluated for any tool called after a closing signal in the same round — the tools still execute, only their effect on the call record is dropped. An order really created, paid for and sent to the kitchen is invisible to the call record: order_id null, outcome abandoned, SMS cost missing. It also contradicts the file's own stated invariant that nothing after the signal is executed. The obvious one-line fix is insufficient because the outcome was evaluated before place_order ran, producing an incoherent row rather than a merely incomplete one.

nodes.label: otp-per-ip-limit-keyed-on-client-supplied-header (MEDIUM, confirmed)
nodes.rationale: There is effectively no per-IP OTP limit: the key comes from the first element of the request's own X-Forwarded-For, and with no proxy in front the header is absent so the limiter never runs at all.
